content: Eosinophilic refers to the property of certain tissues, cells, or organelles that have an affinity for the acidic dye eosin, which is used in histological staining. The term eosinophilic literally means loves eosin, indicating that these structures readily take up the dye. Eosin is an acidic dye, and it binds to basic (or positively charged) structures within cells and tissues. When applied, eosin imparts a bright pink coloration to these components, which typically include the cytoplasm of cells and extracellular proteins such as collagen. Eosinophilic structures are generally composed of proteins. In histology, eosin is most commonly used in combination with another stain called hematoxylin. Together, they form the hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stain, which is the most widely utilized staining method in medical diagnostics. For instance, when a pathologist examines a biopsy sample to evaluate for suspected cancer, the tissue section is typically stained with H&E to enhance visualization of cellular and tissue structures. Certain intracellular structures are also described as eosinophilic due to their ability to take up eosin. Examples of such structures include Lewy bodies, which are associated with neurodegenerative diseases, and Mallory bodies, which are seen in liver pathology.
